pr_body:
This implements the ability to use `require` on `.mjs` files, loaded via the `esm` loader, using the same tradeoffs that [top level await](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-top-level-await) makes in `esm` itself. 

What this means: If possible, all execution and evaluation is done _synchronously_, via immediately unwrapping the execution's component promises. This means that any and all existing code should have no observable change in behavior, as there exist no asynchronous modules as of yet. The catch is that once a module which requires asynchronous execution is used, it must yield to the event loop to perform that execution, which, in turn, can allow other code to execute before the continuation after the async action, which is observable to callers of the now asynchronous module. If this matters to your callers, this means making your module execution asynchronous could be considered a breaking change to your library, however in practice, it will not matter for most callers. Moreover, as the ecosystem exists today, there are _zero_ asynchronously executing modules, and so until there are, there are no downsides to this approach _at all_, as no execution is changed from what one would expect today (excepting, ofc, that it's no longer an error to `require("./foo.mjs")`.

As of right now, this is missing:
* Support for `"type": "module"` in the cjs loader. (where did that go? I thought we already had something that did that internally - `getPackageType` or something?)
* New tests (I have no idea how to write tests for `node`, help appreciated)
* Speculative integration tests for https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/30370 - the code is already written assuming `ModuleWrap.evaluate` may eventually return a promise.

You have an example? TLA can already trivially deadlock in a huge number of ways (there's an [faq entry defending it](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-top-level-await#does-top-level-await-increase-the-risk-of-deadlocks)), what are you thinking of?

@weswigham literally any async behaviour that isn't a one-shot call to a libuv api. interestingly we had an issue opened a few days ago asking about deasync behaviour, you might find it interesting: https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/30634

i'm not entirely familiar with how these libraries work, there are more details of weirdness in #30634 and the deasync repo.

there are several unsolved compatibility issues listed, and unless you could *prove* they're all fixed and that no new ones would pop up, i don't see how we can use this approach.

> there are several unsolved compatibility issues listed, and unless you could prove they're all fixed and that no new ones would pop up, i don't see how we can use this approach.

Aside: you can't _prove_ software is bug free, per sey, you can just test extensively to increase the your confidence that faults likely don't exist~

Also, this is a much, much higher level primitive than `deasync` exposed - this is essentially just an off-brand `await`, implemented in the c++ engine that attempts to avoid spinning event loop turns, if possible. `deasync` left people to compose their own `sync` methods, which often meant that exceptions weren't handled and got left hanging (and you do have to explicitly unwrap the exception out of the promise and rethrow it into the context to get it right, which is a notable thing missing in may of those issues). IMO, `deasync`'s [implementation](https://github.com/abbr/deasync/blob/master/index.js#L34) is also crazy roundabout, since it relies on node-style-continuation callbacks, and quietly fails if the callback isn't actually node-style (eg, error is swapped, the the return value is the error). By only unwrapping promises, this is way, way simpler. And a solid half of it's issues are just related to it being a native module that doesn't always build when the node api changes.

I'm off topic - we shouldn't be discussing an external library that does a kinda-similarish-but-not-really thing to what some internals are doing in this PR. We should be looking to increase confidence in this PR with concrete tests that help us believe it's good, or provide concrete testable examples as to why it's not.

> I don't believe node's own APIs are compatible with the feature introduced here

I don't believe node's whole ecosystem is reasonably compatible with es modules _without_ the feature introduced here.
deasync internals and this pr do the same thing, even if the c++ is slightly different. I'm pointing to previous examples of this approach as being inherently unstable for generalized use in node.

> deasync internals and this pr do the same thing

`deasync` internals just exports raw `uv_run`, which is absolutely not what this is doing - this has a fair bit more around that to handle unwrapping and executing promises appropriately (and actually checking loop completion state), all of which is also only doable in the c++ layer. `node` internals safely use `uv_run` elsewhere - it's a matter of maintaining the expected usage of the event loop - as is, this is way closer to what the platform is already doing in `node_main_instance.cc` (including using the caller's environment's loop, rather than the "default" loop, something `deasync` failed to do, which is likely the cause of the issue with `Worker`s).

> With this change, innocent looking code would be able to trigger error events before event listeners have been added etc..

Only if that code comes from an es module. And es modules can already do that amongst themselves, thanks to TLA. Ergo, nothing has changed there. This is just porting the ability to utilize that behavior to the cjs resolver, which is _immensely_ useful for compatibility.

> Ergo, nothing has changed there.

This is not true. You say "there's a way to do something that's a bit similar in ESM across different file executions!" and then you conclude "so if this happens in the middle of a statement in CJS, even though this was never possible in CJS or anywhere else, nothing has changed!". This absolutely, 100%, changes something fundamental about the execution of synchronous code in any JavaScript running in node. Sync await is something that is currently, by design, not a thing in JS. This PR allows writing a pure JS version of sync await.

Pointing to some examples of scheduling execution of files in the ES module loader is besides the point. Yes - across files or across separate function invocations, JS runtimes usually make no guarantees about execution. No need to look at TLA for that, you could also quote async script tags that also may skip ticks between file executions. But that is not the same thing as departing from run to completion as the basic execution semantic of JS runtimes.

> node internals safely use uv_run elsewhere - it's a matter of maintaining the expected usage of the event loop

afaik we never use uv_run to cause any api that is async to appear synchronous within the same loop. every occurrence should either be entry into evaluation or running a separate loop.

> If I'm reading this right, this would change completion semantics so that source texts can resolve async events that occur after the start of their source but prior to their first await and likewise between awaits and/or between an end or source text.

It's not that there's _no_ await... Just like with TLA, the `await` only appears in the usage module, and not in the modules which import it.

> The framing of not changing anything does not appear to be true

It's less about "not changing anything" and moreso that the behavior is the same as in esm. Namely:
* All sync module execution is still sync
* Only an es module can introduce async execution (via TLA)
* Using an async es module doesn't require `await`
* When an async module is encountered, the event loop may turn, in the middle of an otherwise sync module execution graph

From the perspective of an es module, nothing about the observable behavior for consumers is new. The syntax is different, since the entrypoint is cjs, (`require` vs `import`), but the results are the same, given the same es module structure.

> I'm not ok with this PR if we don't have tests

Well, yeah. As I asked in the OP, how does one go about adding new tests in node (I'm not exactly a regular node contributor)? Both js ones and c++ ones. I am but a wee first time contributor and need help here. Is there, like, a wiki page or doc or something?

@addaleax
> If this ever happens, making that support official would have to be a first step, imo.

Looking at the libuv repo, it looks like someone brought up officially supporting it a few months ago, but at the time, a maintainer decided the additional complexity wasn't yet warranted, and added a doc note instead. So two questions:

1. If this feature is desirable in the end, does that meet the bar for justifying a change in libuv, and
2. Can said complexity be lowered by, rather than supporting reentrant `uv_run` as was originally asked/assumed, introducing a _new_ API function, just for the reentrant `RUN_ONCE` case? This way the function doesn't need to detect if it's a reentrant usage or not (as the caller should already know).

@devsnek
> every occurrence should either be entry into evaluation or running a separate loop.

I could always go back to executing the es module graph in a new event loop; but I think within the same event loop more closely matches how TLA works already in es modules, and removes the deadlock risk of an es module's TLA depending (non-circularly) on an event fired from cjs (tbh, that's probably still an ok trade-off, since that only happens if someone reexposes a cjs context promise to esm, and is probably at least a documentable drawback, but I think it's probably worth pursuing this first, if possible).

> With the caveat that the result must be serializable as JSON, you can do the same today using `execSync`:

I think there's a misunderstanding of what `execSync` does. It's spawning a separate process that shares no state with the node process and is effectively equivalent to a sleep. No userland JS code in the calling thread will ever execute while `execSync` runs. The code you posted would throw because `s._f` is not defined within the newly spawned node process.
that would make more moving to TLA a breaking change, which would be bad. it's currently an implementation detail of a module.

> that would make more moving to TLA a breaking change, which would be bad. it's currently an implementation detail of a module.

Using TLA is already potentially a breaking change, as the extra event loop ticks are observable. 🤷‍♂ 

It'd still be a great deal better than any and all esm being a breaking change to your cjs consumers - especially since _most_ libraries will never need a top level await, tbh.

> Without require(esm), the way that import statements work make it perfectly safe to have TLA in the dependency tree. With the restriction above about patterns that weren't safe in the first place.

Erm, without `require(esm)`, a cjs consumer can't have TLA in it's dependency tree at all. TLA/wasm modules also can't be fully down-compiled for cjs, so if you use either your are necessarily breaking all cjs consumers.

The `whatwg` browser working group has discussed [forbidding TLA in certain browser contexts already, namely service workers](https://github.com/w3c/ServiceWorker/issues/1407) - forbidding TLA modules from cjs entrypoints would not be wholly without precedent.

@weswigham if TLA was banned and we did Atomics.lock style off thread/isolated resolution it seems plausible we wouldn't need to have a sync resolver and we wouldn't need to have a nested event loop. That might be a direction to modify the approach here. The performance profile would be different certainly than an async loading operation but I don't think it changes run semantics in any observable way to my quick thinking about it.

> if TLA was banned and we did Atomics.lock style off thread/isolated resolution it seems plausible we wouldn't need to have a sync resolver and we wouldn't need to have a nested event loop.

Right - I was considering that as a direction to take this if the tradeoffs here or with a nested event loop were unpalatable. But it's best to start with the maximal thing, work through all the objections that can be worked through until there's a completely blocking issue; after all, I think it'd be nice if TLA could work, too. If all I need to do to get that is get libuv to adopt an API they've already considered in the past and convince some people that the different `require` call semantics for TLA'd esm isn't so bad; that's not really that bad. But yeah - there is still a fallback here that's quite capable.

@weswigham I think part of the problem will likely convincing people that https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-jobs-and-job-queues is still preserved. I believe it is not preserved and do want tests explicitly about the divergence with it. It might require much more than a few people if we end up having to upstream changes.

> Erm, without require(esm), a cjs consumer can't have TLA in it's dependency tree at all.

Yes, I was talking about about `import(esm)` and `import esm`. Which are APIs that provide safe access to the async module system.

I'm not sure what "if you're down-compiling for cjs" means in this context. If you use TLA, you can't down-compile to CJS, true. But `require(esm)` would apply to people who make a conscious choice *not* to down-compile. Otherwise we wouldn't need `require(esm)`.

@jkrems 
_Without_ `require(esm)`, your only option to support cjs consumers is to transpile your code to cjs. Top-level `await` cannot be transpiled to `cjs` (it requires actions that cannot be replicated in userland without total control of the module loader, and even then, you can't unwrap a promise synchronously in userland, so the best you can manage is making every module look async). Ergo, if you use top-level await, you cannot support `cjs` consumers. Ergo, if `require(esm)` ends up not supporting top level await, nothing is different in that regard - using top-level `await` is still a breaking change for your cjs consumers. The difference is that using any other esm _isn't_ (and do remember: the primary usecase for TLA is entrypoints and scripts - the vast majority of libraries have no need for it), and you only end up loading one copy of your sources at runtime, which is _much_ more efficient.

>  believe it is not preserved and do want tests explicitly about the divergence with it. It might require much more than a few people if we end up having to upstream changes.

If I were to phrase it in terms of suspending the currently executing job, removing it form the job queue, and then resuming it later once the other jobs are complete (which is exactly what that says the first step of `RunJobs` is, ergo what is already happening by default upon reentrancy), would that be better?

> If I were to phrase it in terms of suspending the currently executing job, removing it form the job queue, and then resuming it later once the other jobs are complete (which is exactly what that says the first step of RunJobs is, ergo what is already happening by default upon reentrancy), would that be better?

It is only removing 1 execution context, which does not match up with that description. The execution context stack is more akin to Function frames than entire Jobs.

> Ergo, if require(esm) ends up not supporting top level await, nothing is different in that regard - using top-level await is still a breaking change for your cjs consumers.

What is different is that you may have CJS consumers if `require(esm)` is a thing. Let's say I'm writing library A. I'm only exposing ESM. I don't care about CJS support. Library B uses A. Library C uses B. Library D uses C. Every one along the line doesn't really care about CJS support. Some unwitting consumer with a CJS app starts using library D. With `require(esm)`, they can! But they may not realize what they just did: They are now at the mercy of... me. Somebody who doesn't write CJS and doesn't care about CJS. They may have a very hard time moving away from library D. And I may have a very hard time accepting that I can't use a perfectly normal ESM feature just because somebody 4 layers down was using my library from CJS.

The alternative is the status quo: Since library A-D are all purely ESM, the app owner never would've started depending on it if they cared about keeping their code in CJS. I won't break any CJS consumers because I don't have any. I consider the lack of an uncanny valley a good thing here: It either works or doesn't work. I never kinda works but breaks if somebody does something that's perfectly reasonable.
@jkrems "I'd rather break absolutely everyone now" doesn't seem terribly compelling over "maybe breaking some people maybe in the future" to me.
Like, that's quite literally an argument for a python 2 -> 3 style ecosystem split, with no real compatibility at all.

> It is only removing 1 execution context, which does not match up with that description. The execution context stack is more akin to Function frames than entire Jobs.

Would it then be theoretically acceptable to explicitly suspend the active execution context and save off the current execution context stack before resuming with an empty one, then? The spec does explicitly state

> However, some ECMAScript features require non-LIFO transitions of the running execution context.

I do not believe so, we are having some chatter in channels but there appears to be a quite explicit:

> No other Job may be initiated until the currently running Job completes. However, the currently running Job or external events may cause the enqueuing of additional PendingJobs that may be initiated sometime after completion of the currently running Job.

https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-jobs-and-job-queues . `to completion` does not appear to imply any sort of preemption/pause being a form of completion currently is the thinking. The LIFO does apply to things like `yield`/`await`/`yield*` though, correct. However, those do run to completion still per providing a completion independent of the resumption of their execution context like https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-generatoryield . There however is some poor wording going on here and we can always seek clarification at a full on meeting.

> "I'd rather break absolutely everyone now"

I'm not suggesting to break anybody. I'm suggesting not introducing an API that breaks people in the future. Reading between your lines, it sounds like you're saying that there's plenty of "perfectly working" ESM code in the ecosystem. And they are required by CJS code. I don't believe that's true. That ESM code is usually not valid ESM but rather "CJS with import sugar". It's code that uses patterns starting from named imports from CJS, references to CJS APIs like `__filename`, all the way to using `require` in random functions because it's more convenient for lazy loading.

I don't think that there's code to break (at scale), so I don't think that my take is "let's break everyone". Nobody is require'ing actual ESM today.
^ this is the reason node doesn't use the `module` field of package.json. i tend to call them "babel modules" since they are often incompatible with real native esm.

Nobody with a `cjs` module today can depend on an es module in node. That means shipping only esm is a break. It doesn't need to be. That break can be moved _significantly_ down the feature+time line (and for the vast majority of packages, eliminated entirely).

> Nobody is require'ing actual ESM today.

[Oh?](https://www.npmjs.com/package/esm) I think that's a kind of willfull blindness to the (exceedingly large) community of people that exist who have been using es module syntax for years already. The people who would be more than happy to adopt a native solution, provided it meets enough of their expectations. I think moving closer to those expectations is a good thing for the ecosystem.

Shipping only ESM is breaking all CJS consumers on node 10 and probably many on node 12. It will also break bundlers etc that don’t support ESM. It’ll be a long while until a package can just remove CJS in a patch version. And even then it would be a questionable use of semver.

> Shipping only ESM is breaking all CJS consumers on node 10 and probably many on node 12. It will also break bundlers etc that don’t support ESM. It’ll be a long while until a package can just remove CJS in a patch version.

It would mean packages only concerned with supporting the latest `node` could upgrade to `esm` as a patch.

It means that even if `node` can't change quickly, that `npm` or `yarn` could have, say, smarter downloads for faster installs. On node 12-13+, `npm` could choose to only down the `esm` sources, if a package provides both an `esm` build and `cjs` build for older versions of node.

It means that adopting `esm` won't cause runtime performance to _plummet_ in projects of any real size because there's two copies of every dual-mode package being loaded into the runtime.

> It means that adopting esm won't cause runtime performance to *plummet* in projects of any real size because there's two copies of every dual-mode package being loaded into the runtime.

Can we please either agree that this is a straw man (realistically only a tiny percentage of total dependencies of a given app will actually have two instances loaded) or can you elaborate what kind of coding patterns you have in mind that would lead to this scenario?

> It means that even if node can't change quickly, that npm or yarn could have, say, smarter downloads for faster installs. On node 12-13+, npm could choose to only down the esm sources, if a package provides both an esm build and cjs build for older versions of node.

This feels highly speculative. Is there any evidence that this is likely to happen as opposed to the already announced lazy/by-file download concepts actually publicized by npm? It feels like those would make this split obsolete.

> It would mean packages only concerned with supporting the latest node could upgrade to esm as a patch.

Those packages will likely have few users and could also just force their users to use ESM to import if they already force their users to be on very specific node versions and toolchains.

@jkrems why is broader compatibility and applicability of es modules such an issue for you? What is inherently _wrong_ with wanting to `require` another module, regardless of format, once the actual implementation issue is gone? Because it doesn't seem like you're arguing about the actual implementation, but rather why you don't think cjs `require` should have access to esm at all.

> elaborate what kind of coding patterns you have in mind that would lead to this scenario?

My package is written in esm. I depend on dep A, and dep B. Both depend on dep C, which has a large tree of dependencies. Dep C is dual mode (as are all it's dependencies, because they care about compatability). Dep A is still written in cjs only, while dep B is written in esm. Now all of dep C's dependency tree is loaded twice, as when I import dep A I load a cjs dependency tree, while with dep B I load an esm one.

Without `require(esm)`, loading any `cjs` only package becomes a footgun that could double your overhead.

> why is broader compatibility and applicability of es modules such an issue for you?

It's not. There's nothing inherently wrong with wanting to `require` ESM. I never argued against the feature request. My main points are:

1. We shouldn't allow a sync operation (e.g. a JS function call) to process async work. At least not if it runs async userland code in the same isolate.
2. A major feature of `import` is the ability to do async work.
3. There are well-established patterns (like dual-publish) that are used today to support `require` and `import` consumers. So there is no "nothing can work if we don't have `require(esm)`" urgency to this feature.

Would I prefer `require(esm)`, everything else being the same? Absolutely! Do I think it's worth giving up on standard JS runtime semantics of async work in node? Absolutely not. Do I think it's worth giving up a useful ESM feature (TLA)? Rather unlikely. Do I think it's worth giving up on reliable async resource loading? It'd be tough.

There's a huge gap between "I'm willing to drop everything to get it" and "I'm actively opposed to this feature".
as long as it was brought up, @std/esm is still "babel modules", and it also doesn't support proper TLA. Might as well just use @std/esm if that's what you're after.

> Do I think it's worth giving up a useful ESM feature (TLA)? Rather unlikely.

The primary usecase for TLA is top-level scripts and such, which, ofc, would be unaffected. TLA is, minimally, detectable by consumers, so can break them all the same and, the workaround if we went the route of forbidding it for `require(esm)`, would be to issue an error that says "use `import` instead of `require` for this module" (which then ofc has a promise to `then` off of). It would just extend the surface area of modules which could silently be upgraded to esm without breaking people (to _most_ modules because, again, _most_ libraries do not need TLA, as TLA is mostly for entrypoints).

> My package is written in esm. I depend on dep A, and dep B. Both depend on dep C, which has a large tree of dependencies. Dep C is dual mode (as are all it's dependencies, because they care about compatability). Dep A is still written in cjs only, while dep B is written in esm. Now all of dep C's dependency tree is loaded twice, as when I import dep A I load a cjs dependency tree, while with dep B I load an esm one. Loading any cjs only package becomes a footgun that could double your overhead.

In your example there's two assumption:

1. A single package's dependency tree is absolutely dominating the app. Every single one of its deps (and its own code) is published as dual-mode.
2. This one package happens to be both require'd and import'd.

Are you suggesting that this is a common case? I have a hard time coming up with an app that could look like this. It's an express app where the majority of its size is just express and express is added twice..? From all `npm ls` I've seen, it doesn't feel like a likely tree. Is this really a structure you've witnessed?

> The primary usecase for TLA is top-level scripts and such, which, ofc, would be unaffected.

I disagree. It's also super useful for loading config files, initializing resources, etc.. Many of which are currently using `readFileSync` & friends. That code could move to more event-loop-friendly patterns with async/await (at least sibling trees could execute instead of a global stop-the-world).

>Are you suggesting that this is a common case

Yes. Package C could trivially be `lodash`,`gulp`, `webpack`, or any number of other packages critical to the ecosystem, while A and B are plugins/augmentations thereupon. And the problem only gets _worse_ over time - the more packages that ship dual mode, the worse the problem gets, right up until _everything_ is dual mode (and so has an esm implementation), at which point you _finally_ only have one copy of your dependency tree. It makes having a `cjs`-only dependency toxic to performance.

> I disagree. It's also super useful for loading config files, initializing resources, etc.. Many of which are currently using readFileSync & friends. That code could move to more event-loop-friendly patterns with async/await (at least sibling trees could execute instead of a global stop-the-world).

Sure, it's useful - if you actually need it. Not many packages do that at the top level outside of some kind of `startup` function or constructor. While possible, it's arguably an antipattern, precisely because it can't be done async today (and so most packages do not). For every package you could find me with a top level `readFileSync`, I could give you a hundred with no top-level fs operations (or other potentially async-able operations) at all. And when those cases crop up (which as of today is zero cases, mind you, since TLA isn't actually in yet) saying "sorry cjs consumer, you're going to need to use `import` and deal with the async-ness in some way" would not be bad. The only thing that would be better from the consumers' perspective would be, well, this as-is, with the attempt to execute the async operations in-line.

> "sorry cjs consumer, you're going to need to use import and deal with the async-ness in some way" would not be bad

Right, but you're back to assuming that the package in question had any direct CJS consumers. If the CJS consumer has to open bugs against/communicate with maintainers of 4 layers of intermediate ESM packages, the whole thing stops being quite so reasonable.

> Yes. Package C could trivially be lodash,gulp, webpack, or any number of other packages critical to the ecosystem, while A and B are plugins/augmentations thereupon.

But any package with plugins/augmentations... wouldn't be able to publish a dual mode package. So either it has a reason to be loaded from multiple places (because plugins augment it) *or* it's likely to be a true dual mode package. And `lodash` doesn't have dependencies. Only a tiny subset of `webpack` is likely required by plugins, none of which will likely pull in some sort of huge dep tree. Same for `gulp`. Gulp plugins don't pull in a huge shared dependency tree. They pull in that weird file/stream abstraction library at most which isn't a huge dep tree. So - I'm sorry but package C could *not* be trivially lodash, gulp, webpack. Maybe there's a non-trivial way it could be one of those packages but not the setups I'm aware of.

> And lodash doesn't have dependencies

But is, itself, a huge, wide tree of modules (which is why deep imports to specific functions are sometimes preferred).

> Only a tiny subset of webpack is likely required by plugins, none of which will likely pull in some sort of huge dep tree. 

If your plugin is `Tapable` (and it probably is), you'll pull in all of `webpack` and it's deps, as that's defined in the core of `webpack`, and you need to inherit from it.

> Gulp plugins don't pull in a huge shared dependency tree

When they wrap `gulp` like `gulp-help`, which is in most any good gulpfile, they have to include all of it. Likewise, any package providing tasks will end up including `gulp` as a whole to use the default `gulp` instance to add the tasks. And its dependency tree is quite large - it's not just it's custom vfs and stream utils, but its logging intrastructure, async execution infrastructure, task scheduler, and more (the gulp dependency chain very much follows the "package should have a single responsibility" principle).

> Right, but you're back to assuming that the package in question had any direct CJS consumers

Literally every package that exists today, with little exception (for those who like to ship things that don't work without flags or tools), has cjs consumers. I don't think assuming packages have and will have cjs consumers so long as they can is that unreasonable of an assumption.
No pure ESM package has CJS consumers today. And I was talking about a pure ESM package.

I think we can all agree that if there were an easy way to achieve require
esm without any of these issues that we would want it.

The problem is more simply that as it stands this PR is not mergable since
it is clearing the task queue when you run require(), which should only
ever be triggered on execution completion (eg Promises don’t resolve while
a require is executing).

In terms of enforcing a sync esm loading pipeline there are still more
concerns such as that custom loaders that fetch from URLs would block the
entire JS thread during that fetch for all esm loads, and that is
potentially not a door we want to close.

Wesley, if you are able to respond to these concerns over timings with
valid counter approaches that could be a possible step forward.

Echoing @guybedford, I think we'd all love to have a more compatible world with easy migration, so thank you for trying to assist this @weswigham. Unfortunately it seems like `require(ESM)` is not possible without violating important invariants regarding the event loop and microtasks.

Here's an example:

```js
// unwrap-p.mjs
export let value = await globalThis.p.then(x = > x.json());
```

```js
// main.js
globalThis.p = fetch("http://...");                      // create a promise
let fetchedJsonValue = require("./unwrap-p.mjs").value;  // synchronously unwrap the promise!
```

The ability to require `.mjs` files implies the ability to pause the event loop and synchronously unwrap promises.  That is a significant new capability provided in this PR that is not provided by Top-Level Await, therefore it is not [making the same trade-offs](https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/30891#issue-351626498).

Importantly, this new ability violates the [Promises/A+ requirement 2.2.4](https://promisesaplus.com/#point-34) that states fulfillment handlers must only run when the stack is exhausted.

> the ability to pause the event loop and synchronously unwrap promises

This is similar to `node-fibers` and some of the magic it can do, for example in Meteor’s `unwrapAsync`. This PR could potentially become another userland NPM module like `node-fibers`, that would be free to break spec. I know that’s not as useful as having it in core, but it’s another option between having it in core and not having it at all.

> Every call site of require() needs every execution context to be in a yield position

Just to make sure the scope of this is clear: `require` is a function call that currently may exist in *any* expression position, not only in the top-most function body. So a more extreme way to put it would be "if require calls turn into a yield expression, all functions running in node would have to become generators". "All functions" may be too broad but given how dynamic JS is, it's pretty close.

So I would say: Yes, there is something spec-wise to prevent it. Because that transformation would realistically also apply to all "real"/spec'd JS (ES modules), not just to CJS. Otherwise call sites into functions that use inline-`require` would break. That's of course unless there would be a way to isolate CJS being called from JS code.
There’s also makeRequireFunction in ESM that would need to act the same as CJS require.

One thing that we ran out of time for in our call: If the idea is that `require(esm)` can run a syncified version of the entire module loading pipeline, how does this affect concurrent import jobs? E.g. say an import job is currently active that touches on a subset of the same modules involved in the required esm. What happens to that job? Do we somehow prevent that job to yield back to the event loop? If so, how? Or would we effectively say that all import jobs become synchronous (in relation to the main thread) and accept that loading and compiling code in the background is no longer a feature of ESM that node supports?

> // wants to reuse import job for a but that job is currently set up to yield back to the main thread

I don't understand this, the each ModuleJob is independent and only the entire graph yields back (though I'm unclear on the "yield back" phrasing).

> // What does it do? Does it modify the original job? Does it synchronously set the job's resolutions?

Modify and resolve, both synchronously. I'm unclear on the problem being framed with that as ModuleJob is not a Promise in and of itself.

> // Also implied: Does this mean that everything to do with import needs to happen in C++?

Not to my knowledge

> I don't understand this, the each ModuleJob is independent and only the entire graph yields back (though I'm unclear on the "yield back" phrasing).

Yield back as "allow JS to run on the main thread". JS can run on the main thread while a file is loading for example. The way the module job is currently written, we do yield control of the main thread all the time, not just when the entire module graph has been loaded. Which means that the individual steps that need to run on the main thread (like creating objects in the Isolate) have to be scheduled somehow. Right now we use promises to do it. If we don't call them, nothing happens.

So if we can't use promises to schedule those main thread units of work, what is the replacement? Will we have a separate scheduler that needs to be called from the main event loop but also can be called blocking?

> I'm unclear on the problem being framed with that as ModuleJob is not a Promise in and of itself.

The module job isn't a Promise but uses Promises to schedule work. That's why I used "resolutions" - a job depends on many resolutions right now, one for each time it needs to do work on the main thread.

> So if we can't use promises to schedule those main thread units of work, what is the replacement? 

ESM graph execution actually isn't "scheduled" at all yet. It's 100% sync (as TLA isn't actually in yet). And, to be clear: to be to spec for TLA, you _can't_ naively hook it up with just chained promises, or you don't preserve sync module graphs, which is required. Not that any of that really matters, since v8 wires up all the executions anyway - we just call `.execute` on the root v8 module object. Today, that's always sync. Post-TLA, it'll return a promise or not. The non-promise return will indicate execution was purely sync, the promise return'll indicate async execution was required. We can then return that promise or throw (which seems preferable based on today's discussion) as desired. All that `ModuleJob` scheduling chicanery is actually handled by v8 itself - we just kick it off by specifying an entrypoint (and doing the resolution).

> The module job isn't a Promise but uses Promises to schedule work. That's why I used "resolutions" - a job depends on many resolutions right now, one for each time it needs to do work on the main thread.

Yes and no. It does right now, but it doesn't _need_ to. It's implemented as such to be API forward compatible with potential in-thread async resolver hooks; but those are problematic for other reasons, so running them off-thread (and simplifying the API to not be unnecessarily async tagged) is nicer anyway (plus, the API is internal anyway, so it was a bit of a premature over-design).

> ESM graph execution actually isn't "scheduled" at all yet.

I wasn't talking about execution, I was talking about load and compile. My graph above ended with a single execute but I maybe should've been clear that it was only included for illustrative purposes as "the thing happening after the whole process is over". :)

> All that ModuleJob scheduling chicanery is actually handled by v8 itself - we just kick it off by specifying an entrypoint (and doing the resolution).

It's not, the module job is handled by the embedder which in this case is us. We lifted the name "module job" from the HTML spec which is implemented in Chrome/Blink. V8 has no orchestration for resolution and resource loading built-in afaik.

> Yes and no. It does right now, but it doesn't need to.

That's what I wrote above. :) But I also mentioned very specific advantages for allowing fetch&compile to happen while execution of the main thread continues. It's not just "because we can". It's because it's a known issue with `require` that blocking the main thread while dependencies load and parse can be costly. At least from my side running async resolvers in-thread was never a goal.

issue_context.title: Cannot use mjs file synchronously in commonJS without await / .then()
issue_context.body:
* **Version**: v12.17.0
* **Platform**: Linux
* **Subsystem**: Ubuntu

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

Require an mjs file.

```js
const isPromise = require('./third-party-is-promise.mjs')

console.log(typeof isPromise)
```

Example https://gist.github.com/Raynos/2c6bb0a8537dbf7d464a9b85813cd3b1

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Always

### What is the expected behavior?

I can load an ESM module from a commonJS file.

### What do you see instead?

```sh
~/tmp/temp123
$ node broken.cjs 
internal/modules/cjs/loader.js:984
    throw new ERR_REQUIRE_ESM(filename);
    ^

Error [ERR_REQUIRE_ESM]: Must use import to load ES Module: /home/raynos/tmp/temp123/third-party-is-promise.mjs
    at Module.load (internal/modules/cjs/loader.js:984:11)
    at Function.Module._load (internal/modules/cjs/loader.js:879:14)
    at Module.require (internal/modules/cjs/loader.js:1026:19)
    at require (internal/modules/cjs/helpers.js:72:18)
    at Object.<anonymous> (/home/raynos/tmp/temp123/broken.cjs:1:19)
    at Module._compile (internal/modules/cjs/loader.js:1138:30)
    at Object.Module._extensions..js (internal/modules/cjs/loader.js:1158:10)
    at Module.load (internal/modules/cjs/loader.js:986:32)
    at Function.Module._load (internal/modules/cjs/loader.js:879:14)
    at Function.executeUserEntryPoint [as runMain] (internal/modules/run_main.js:71:12) {
  code: 'ERR_REQUIRE_ESM'
}
```

### Additional information

I would like to import an ESM synchronously from a commonJS file.

Node added `child_process.execSync()` a while ago but that used to not be possible.

It would be really nice if node had some kind of `importSync()` feature.

I also tried

```js
const isPromise = import('./third-party-is-promise.mjs')

console.log(typeof isPromise)
console.log('then method', typeof isPromise.then)
```

This returns a promise instead of the code which is not what I want

Those who use `@snek/syncify` are doomed to a life of sadness

More realistically, if you're looking for a way to "bottle up" promises and resolve them synchronously, you should look into `node-fibers` and its use in the framework Meteor. That's at least one example of doing so in a widely used framework that has many production apps. Meteor (at least currently) only supports ESM by transpiling it to CommonJS, however; it's unclear whether it can ever support native ESM along with `node-fibers`. Based on the discussion in https://github.com/nodejs/modules/issues/454, such a thing might not be possible, or possible without violating spec (which is something that Node can't do).

The ECMAScript spec does actually provide data on if top level await is used: https://tc39.es/proposal-top-level-await/#sec-cyclic-module-records in a new internal `[[Async]]` slot, however this is set for more than just top level await; all WASM modules have that as `true` due to their initialization lifecycle as I understand. This internal slot is not currently reflected in V8's public API though to my knowledge. I think we could review this if/when it is exposed as a means to help transitioning.

Could you explain more about the limitations of loading a WASM module synchronously ? 

I think `require(mjs)` and `require(wasm)` are two completely different beasts.

I would be fine with a `require(mjs)` that fails on transitive dependencies that use Top level await and WASM.

The fast majority of the uses cases for ESM is trivial code that doesn't do anything special with top level await or WASM.

review_comments: so this just skips the esm resolver entirely? this seems like a rather dangerous divergence.

That's because we already resolved the specifier, in order to know we needed the esm loader. The cjs resolver and the esm resolver are _supposed_ to resolve the same specifier to the same thing, so it _should_ be fine. This is part of why I kept saying it _really should only be considered to be one loader_.
